bounded_slice.candidate: RFC 9052 COSE_Sign1 as a self-contained offline persistence envelope for evidence bytes and signature metadata

primary_source.title: RFC 9052: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Structures and Process

bounded_slice.tested_scope: Static inspection of exactly one official RFC Editor primary source, RFC 9052. Tested only whether a COSE_Sign1 object can persist evidence payload bytes plus signature/header metadata so the archived object can later be signature-verified after HTTP transport without preserving live HTTP message state. No second public source, implementation execution, external service, protected-primary action, manual-user execution, or scheduler mutation was consumed.
observations: COSE_Sign1 carries protected headers, unprotected headers, a payload field and a signature field in one CBOR object. When the payload is present rather than detached, the serialized content to be signed is carried inside the object as a bstr.

The signature input Sig_structure includes the protected header bytes, optional external AAD, and the full payload; RFC 9052 states the full payload is used independent of how it is transported. Therefore an archived embedded-payload COSE_Sign1 can be re-verified later without reconstructing HTTP headers, provided the profile uses empty external_aad or archives/reconstructs any nonempty external_aad separately.

Protected header parameters are cryptographically protected. The header map permits application-defined labels, so digest metadata can be carried inside the protected bucket by an application profile, or a digest can be included inside the signed payload. RFC 9052 itself does not define digest semantics for such an application field, so digest meaning/algorithm policy is not closed by this source alone.

COSE_Sign1 signs the exact payload byte string supplied by the application; it does not canonicalize arbitrary evidence structures into those bytes. Stable evidence canonicalization therefore remains a separate child.

Successful verification also requires a verification key and application checks that the key is correctly paired with and authorized for the signing identity. Key trust/distribution is not self-contained merely because the COSE object is self-contained.

This slice establishes later offline re-verifiability of the archived signed object under the stated conditions, not anti-replay/freshness. Replaying a previously valid COSE object can still verify cryptographically unless a higher-level freshness/replay policy rejects it.
bounded_slice.inference: Within this exact specification-level scope, COSE_Sign1 conditionally passes the self-contained offline persistence-envelope child: if evidence bytes are embedded as payload, security-relevant metadata is either inside the signed payload or protected headers, and external_aad is empty or separately reproducible, the archived object contains the payload and signature material needed to reconstruct the signature input after HTTP transport. This does not close deterministic evidence canonicalization, digest semantics, key trust, concrete Chat-native signing/verification, replay-prevention policy, PROV-to-JSON mapping, or observation/inference/uncertainty schema.
bounded_slice.uncertainty: No cryptographic implementation or interoperability test was run. No claim is made that scheduled Chat can create or verify COSE signatures with trusted keys without another execution surface, that a particular digest header profile is standardized here, or that COSE alone prevents replay.
bounded_slice.hidden_executor_absence: specification_layer_only; concrete cryptographic execution and trusted-key handling remain unresolved rather than assumed
bounded_slice.residual_richer_mode_protected_manual_us: 0 for the static specification inspection itself; concrete Chat-native COSE signing/verification and trusted-key handling remain unresolved children and are not claimed solved
bounded_slice.quota_zero_assessment: RFC 9052 defines an offline message/security data structure and processing model and does not inherently require hosted compute, paid service, finite monthly credit, artifact storage, or external API. Actual Chat-native cryptographic execution capability was not tested and is not claimed quota-independently solved.
